scenario: AITA for disagreeing with our HR? | I am a 7 month newly hired employee for a big corporation. Last night our HR sent out a five page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline". Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether disagreeing with HR in this situation is right or wrong. Let me start by understanding the scenario properly. I'm a 7-month newly hired employee at a big corporation. Last night, HR sent out a five-page memo to all employees titled "Office Discipline." They reminded everyone about various office rules, like not loitering during office hours, sticking to lunch schedules, the correct dress code, and wearing IDs at all times. Now, in my 6 months here, HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. The company is large, with an entire floor dedicated to HR, unlike multiple departments sharing one floor. Despite their size, they're slow. It took them about 5 months to process my payroll, so the delay in ID cards isn't a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID started using government-issued IDs to enter the building. But this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. I called HR when I got to my desk to ask for the status of my and my colleagues' IDs. They told me they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swamped with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, giving us a template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for HR's shortcomings by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keeping using whatever IDs we have right now, regardless of what happens next week. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong to disagree with HR in this situation? First, I need to consider the company's policies and the role of HR. HR is responsible for issuing IDs, and their delay in doing so is a failure on their part. By suggesting that employees print their own IDs, HR is essentially shifting their responsibility onto the employees, which is unfair. Employees should not have to bear the cost or effort of producing their own IDs when it's HR's duty to provide them. This could set a bad precedent, where employees are expected to cover for HR's inefficiencies. Moreover, the security measure of noting and reporting employees without IDs seems harsh, especially when HR has been slow to provide the necessary IDs. It's not fair to penalize employees for something that's beyond their control, especially when HR has failed to fulfill their responsibilities. Disagreeing with HR in this case is justified because it's a matter of holding HR accountable for their duties. Employees have the right to expect that HR will provide the necessary resources, and when they fail to do so, it's reasonable to voice concerns and push for a resolution. However, it's also important to approach the disagreement professionally and constructively. Instead of just refusing to comply, it might be better to express the concerns to HR and request that they expedite the process or find an alternative solution. In summary, disagreeing with HR in this situation is right because it's about upholding the employees' rights and ensuring that HR fulfills their responsibilities. It's important to address the issue constructively rather than passively resisting, but standing up for one's rights is justified in this case.
